cdc_long_covid_children_2022_fig1: This is a grouped bar chart depicting percentages of children in the United States in 2022 who have ever had Long COVID or currently have Long COVID, separated by sex. The y-axis represents percentage values ranging from 0 to 3 percent. The x-axis divides the data into two categories: "Ever Long COVID" and "Current Long COVID." The legend shows three groups: Total (dark blue bars), Boys (green bars), and Girls (light blue bars). The chart shows that girls have the highest percentages for both ever having and currently having Long COVID, followed by the total population, with boys having the lowest percentages in both categories. The overall pattern indicates higher Long COVID prevalence among girls compared to boys.
cdc_long_covid_children_2022_fig2: This is a vertical bar chart showing the percentage of children in the United States who have ever had Long COVID or currently have Long COVID in 2022. The y-axis represents the percentage, ranging from 0 to 3 percent. The x-axis has two groups: "Ever Long COVID" and "Current Long COVID." Bars are color-coded by age group: dark blue for 0–5 years, green for 6–11 years, and light gray for 12–17 years. The chart shows higher percentages for older children in both categories, with the 12–17 years group having the highest percentages. The main pattern shows that older children are more affected by Long COVID than younger ones, with current cases being lower than ever cases across all age groups.
cdc_long_covid_children_2022_fig3: This figure is a grouped bar chart showing the percentage of children who ever had Long COVID and who currently have Long COVID in the United States in 2022. The vertical axis represents percent, ranging from 0 to 3 percent. Four racial and ethnic groups are compared, indicated by different colors: Asian, non-Hispanic (dark blue), Black, non-Hispanic (green), White, non-Hispanic (gray), and Hispanic (light green). The horizontal axis shows two categories: Ever Long COVID and Current Long COVID. The main pattern indicates that Hispanic children have the highest percentage of ever having Long COVID, followed by White, Black, and Asian children, while current Long COVID percentages are lower overall, with White children showing the highest current rates.
noaa_sea_ice_2020_fig1: This figure is a pair of polar maps showing monthly average sea ice extent in the Arctic for March 2020 (left) and September 2020 (right). The maps display the Arctic region with landmasses of Russia, Alaska, Canada, Greenland, and Europe labeled. Sea ice extent is shown in white, while open ocean is dark blue, and land is gray. A pink line marks the median ice edge from 1981-2010 for comparison. The main pattern shows extensive sea ice coverage in March 2020, close to the median edge, and much reduced ice extent in September 2020, with the ice edge notably retreating far inside the median boundary. This highlights the seasonal sea ice minimum in September and significant ice loss relative to the 1981-2010 median.
noaa_sea_ice_2020_fig2: This line graph shows monthly sea ice extent percent difference from 1979 to 2020 for March (black) and September (red). The y-axis represents percent difference, ranging from -50 to +50. The x-axis shows years from 1978 to 2020. The legend identifies solid black and red lines for monthly sea ice extent in March and September, respectively, and dashed lines for their linear trends. The graph indicates a relatively stable sea ice extent for March, with a slight declining trend, while September shows a significant decreasing trend in sea ice extent over the period. This figure illustrates the seasonal and long-term changes in sea ice for these two specific months, highlighting increasing summer ice loss.
noaa_sea_ice_2020_fig3: This figure consists of two colored maps and one stacked area chart depicting Arctic sea ice age. The maps show sea ice age coverage in years for the Arctic Ocean during mid-March 1985 (upper left) and 2020 (upper right), using a color scale: blue (0-1 years), light blue (1-2), green (2-3), yellow (3-4), and red (>4 years). The maps highlight sea ice primarily aged 4+ years in 1985, with a notable reduction and concentrated younger ice in 2020. The bottom stacked area chart shows the percentage of sea ice age categories in the Arctic Ocean from 1985 to 2020. The y-axis ranges from 0% to 100%, illustrating a long-term decrease in older ice (3-4, 4+ years) and an increase in younger ice (0-1, 1-2 years), indicating significant sea ice aging decline over 35 years.
noaa_sea_ice_2020_fig4: This figure contains three panels showing Northern Hemisphere sea ice data. Panel (a) is a time series plot with the x-axis representing dates from October 15, 2019, to April 15, 2020, and the y-axis showing sea ice volume in cubic kilometers (0 to 22,000 km³). It includes minimum (blue dashed line), maximum (red dashed line), and average (gray dot-dashed line) daily volumes for winters 2010/11 to 2019/20, with the 2019/20 season in a black solid line surrounded by blue shading indicating below-average volume. Panel (b) is a line graph showing monthly sea ice thickness in meters (0.5 to 3.0 m) from November to April for Winter 2018/19 (blue circles) and Winter 2019/20 (brown squares) in the Inner Arctic, with shaded confidence intervals. Panel (c) shows histograms of sea ice thickness frequency (%) up to 15% for April 2019 and 2020 from ICESat-2 and CryoSat-2 data, with thickness on the x-axis (0-6 m).
noaa_sea_ice_2020_fig5: This figure consists of two color-coded maps of the Arctic region for April 2020. The left map shows sea ice thickness in meters, ranging from 0 (dark blue) to 5 (yellow). The thickness is greatest in central Arctic areas with a gradient decreasing towards the edges. The right map displays the sea ice thickness anomaly relative to the 2011-2019 winter average, in meters, ranging from -1.5 (blue) to +1.5 (red). Notable anomalies include areas of thinner ice (blue) and thicker ice (red) relative to the long-term mean, with a prominent thicker ice anomaly near the eastern side of the Arctic Ocean. Geographic regions include the Arctic Ocean, surrounding seas, Greenland, and northern landmasses. Data is from the CryoSat-2/SMOS multi-sensor product by AWI/ESA.
